steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper that builds a procedural language understanding benchmark for Turkish, as a case study for low-resource languages. Explain what procedural text and PLU are, what earlier wikiHow-based tasks exist, why other languages are left out, and what our benchmark, experiments and findings are.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What procedural text is and why PLU matters
- Prior work on wikiHow and procedural tasks
- The gap: PLU missing for most languages
- Our approach: a Turkish case study and centralized benchmark
- How we built it, what we found, what we release

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What procedural text is and why PLU matters
  - sequence of steps, specific order, accomplish a goal
  - example: caring for an indoor plant: i) location, ii) indoor humidity, iii) right fertilizer; usually in that order
  - needs diverse skills tied to traditional NLP tasks: semantic analysis (who did what to whom), commonsense reasoning (plant requires water), coreference resolution (it -> the plant)
  - so PLU = proxy for performance on a combination of these skills
- Prior work on wikiHow and procedural tasks
  - wikiHow tutorials used heavily; several downstream tasks proposed
  - step and goal inference: predict likely step given goal or vice versa
  - next event prediction given goal and current step
  - both multiple-choice QA; need partial understanding of step-goal relations
  - information retrieval: link steps to related goals -> wikiHow hierarchy
  - abstractive summarization (several works) -> needs competitive generation skills
- The gap: PLU missing for most languages
  - lack of language-specific web corpora
  - all tasks above English-only, except one summarization work
  - creating task data hard; may need language-specific filtering for quality
  - previous works study tasks in isolation -> limited insight into model performance
- Our approach: Turkish case study, centralized benchmark
  - uneven distribution of procedural data across languages
  - goal: inspire PLU research on understudied languages from different families
  - case study on Turkish
  - centralized approach: comprehensive benchmark with six downstream tasks
- How we built it, what we found, what we release
  - automatic machine translation for scarcity; rigorous quality control incl. human evaluation; data is high-quality
  - survey/study downstream tasks; language-specific filtering; manual test data annotation
  - experiments: diverse LMs, different pretraining, fine-tuning settings, architectures
  - language-specific models mostly beat multilingual ones; but model size matters more than training language (large multilingual > medium language-specific)
  - rigorous language-specific preprocessing (e.g. goal inference) -> higher quality, more challenging
  - best models (esp. reranking, goal inference, step ordering) far behind English counterparts -> room for improvement
  - release: corpus of more than 52,000 tutorials, splits for six tasks, baseline models; https://github.com/GGLAB-KU/turkish-plu

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A procedural text is a text that has a sequence of steps, and the steps need to be followed in a certain order to reach a goal. For example, if you want to care for an indoor plant, you need to do things like i) choosing a good location for the plant, ii) keeping the indoor humidity at the right level, and iii) choosing the right fertilizer, and usually in this order. Following step-by-step instructions to reach a goal needs a lot of different skills, and these skills can be related to traditional NLP tasks like semantic analysis (e.g., who did what to whom), commonsense reasoning (e.g., plant requires water) and coreference resolution (e.g., it refers to the plant). So procedural language understanding (PLU) can be seen as a proxy for measuring how well models do on a combination of these different skills.

Previous work used the WikiHow tutorials a lot and proposed several downstream tasks on procedural text. For example, one work introduced step inference and goal inference tasks, where the model should predict the most likely step given the goal, or the goal given the step. Another work proposed predicting the next event given the goal and the current step. All these tasks are multiple-choice QA tasks and they need a partial understanding of the relations between steps and goals in procedural documents. Also, there is an information retrieval task where steps are linked to related goals to create a wikiHow hierarchy. Finally, some other works proposed an abstractive summarization task, which needs competitive language generation skills.

- The gap: PLU missing for most languages
  - lack of language-specific web corpora; all tasks above English-only except one summarization work
  - creating task data hard; may need language-specific filtering for quality
  - previous works study tasks in isolation -> limited insight
- Our approach: Turkish case study
  - uneven distribution of procedural data; inspire PLU research on understudied languages from different families
  - centralized approach: comprehensive benchmark, six downstream tasks
- How we built it, findings, release
  - machine translation + rigorous quality control incl. human evaluation -> high-quality data
  - language-specific filtering, manual test data annotation
  - experiments on diverse LMs (pretraining, fine-tuning settings, architectures)
  - language-specific mostly better, but model size matters more (large multilingual > medium language-specific)
  - goal inference etc. (rigorous preprocessing) -> higher quality, more challenging
  - best models far behind English (esp. reranking, goal inference, step ordering)
  - release: corpus of more than 52,000 tutorials, splits for six tasks, baselines; https://github.com/GGLAB-KU/turkish-plu

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A procedural text is a text that has a sequence of steps, and the steps need to be followed in a certain order to reach a goal. For example, if you want to care for an indoor plant, you need to do things like i) choosing a good location for the plant, ii) keeping the indoor humidity at the right level, and iii) choosing the right fertilizer, and usually in this order. Following step-by-step instructions to reach a goal needs a lot of different skills, and these skills can be related to traditional NLP tasks like semantic analysis (e.g., who did what to whom), commonsense reasoning (e.g., plant requires water) and coreference resolution (e.g., it refers to the plant). So procedural language understanding (PLU) can be seen as a proxy for measuring how well models do on a combination of these different skills.

Previous work used the WikiHow tutorials a lot and proposed several downstream tasks on procedural text. For example, one work introduced step inference and goal inference tasks, where the model should predict the most likely step given the goal, or the goal given the step. Another work proposed predicting the next event given the goal and the current step. All these tasks are multiple-choice QA tasks and they need a partial understanding of the relations between steps and goals in procedural documents. Also, there is an information retrieval task where steps are linked to related goals to create a wikiHow hierarchy. Finally, some other works proposed an abstractive summarization task, which needs competitive language generation skills.

Even though PLU is important, it has been mostly ignored for most languages, because there are not enough language-specific web corpora. All of the tasks above are only available in English, except for one of the summarization works. Besides the lack of raw text, it is also hard to create downstream task data, and it might need language-specific filtering techniques to make sure the quality is high. Finally, all previous works study the tasks they propose in isolation, and this only gives limited insight into how the model performs.

Since procedural data is distributed unevenly across languages, we want to inspire research on PLU for other understudied languages from different language families. For this, we design a case study on Turkish. Different from previous works, we take a centralized approach and introduce a comprehensive benchmark with six downstream tasks on procedural documents.

To deal with the lack of resources, we use automatic machine translation tools. We apply strict quality control for the machine translation, including human evaluation, and we show that the data is high-quality. Next, we survey and study several downstream tasks and we create high-quality and challenging task data with language-specific filtering and manual annotation of the test data. Finally, we run a comprehensive set of experiments on a diverse set of language models that have different pretraining, fine-tuning settings and architectures. We find that language-specific models mostly do better than multilingual ones, but model size is more important than the training language, meaning that large enough multilingual models do better than medium sized language-specific models. We show that the tasks where we can do strict language-specific preprocessing, like goal inference, have higher quality and so are more challenging. We also find that our best models for most downstream tasks, especially reranking, goal inference and step ordering, are still far behind the English ones, which means there is a lot of room for improvement. We release all the resources, including the structured corpus of more than 52,000 tutorials, data splits for the six downstream tasks and the baseline models we experimented with, at https://github.com/GGLAB-KU/turkish-plu.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A procedural text typically consists of a sequence of steps that need to be followed in a specific order to accomplish a goal. For example, to care for an indoor plant, one must carry out tasks such as i) selecting an appropriate location for the plant, ii) maintaining indoor humidity levels, and iii) selecting the right fertilizer, usually in the given order. Accomplishing a goal given with step-by-step instructions requires a set of diverse skills that can be related to traditional NLP tasks such as semantic analysis (e.g., who did what to whom), commonsense reasoning (e.g., plant requires water), and coreference resolution (e.g., it refers to the plant). Hence, procedural language understanding (PLU) can be considered a proxy to measure the performance of models on a combination of these distinct skills.

Previous work has heavily utilized the WikiHow tutorials and proposed several downstream tasks on procedural text. For example, [1] introduced step and goal inference tasks where the objective is to predict the most likely step given the goal or vice versa. Similarly, [2] proposed predicting the next event given the goal and the current step. All of these tasks are formulated as multiple-choice QA and require a partial understanding of step-goal relations in procedural documents. Furthermore, [3] proposed an information retrieval task where steps are linked to related goals to create a wikiHow hierarchy. Finally, several other works [4,5] proposed an abstractive summarization task, which requires competitive language generation skills.

Despite its importance, PLU has been largely ignored for most languages due to a lack of language-specific web corpora. Except for [5], all the aforementioned tasks are only available in English. Besides the scarcity of raw text, creating downstream task data is challenging and might require language-specific filtering techniques to ensure high quality. Finally, all previous works study the proposed tasks in isolation, which gives only limited insight into the model's performance.

Considering the uneven distribution of available procedural data across languages, our objective is to inspire research on PLU for other understudied languages from different language families. To this end, we design a case study focused on Turkish. Unlike previous works, we adopt a centralized approach and introduce a comprehensive benchmark that contains six downstream tasks on procedural documents.

To address the scarcity of resources, we use automatic machine translation tools. We implement rigorous quality control for machine translation, including human evaluation, and show that the data is indeed high-quality. Next, we survey and study several downstream tasks and create high-quality, challenging task data through language-specific filtering and manual test data annotation. Finally, we perform a comprehensive set of experiments on a diverse set of language models with different pretraining, fine-tuning settings, and architectures. We find that language-specific models mostly outperform their multilingual counterparts; however, model size is a more important factor than training language, i.e., large enough multilingual models outperform medium sized language-specific models. We show that tasks where rigorous language-specific preprocessing is possible, such as goal inference, are of higher quality and thus more challenging. Finally, we find that our best-performing models for most downstream tasks, especially reranking, goal inference, and step ordering, are still far behind their English counterparts, which suggests a large room for improvement. We release all resources, including the structured corpus of more than 52,000 tutorials, data splits for six downstream tasks and the baseline models we experimented with, at https://github.com/GGLAB-KU/turkish-plu.
